tracks.title: The compiler runs in the sandbox
tracks.text: Lesson 03 point 3 — lanes. This is a deep dive, under toolkit. [curious] Here's the puzzle it has to answer. Everyone knows you can't run rustc, or LLVM, inside WebAssembly. So how does a toolkit get built in the sandbox? The answer is a thing we call a lane. A lane is one language's path from untrusted text… to runnable wasm… where every executing stage is itself a wasm guest. And each lane is a different trick. This page is the tricks… the convergence… and the honest ceilings.

tracks.title: The compiler is the attack surface
tracks.text: First — the compiler is the attack surface. [curious] Installing software means running a compiler. Building a Rust crate runs build dot rs. Installing an npm package runs an install script. Compiling C runs a driver that spawns a linker. Every one of those is arbitrary code… executing natively… with your permissions… before you've read a line of what you pulled down. The artifact isn't the danger. The build is. And the reflex answer — just wrap it in an OS sandbox — the repo rejects in plain words. A native compile under bwrap, or seatbelt, is not a sufficient boundary for adversarial untrusted source on a shared host. OS sandboxes are defense in depth… not isolation. That gap is exactly why microVMs exist. So the rule here is harder. Untrusted source never compiles, or runs, natively. At all. Which means the compiler itself has to become a wasm guest.

tracks.title: What a lane is
tracks.text: So — what a lane is. A lane is one source language's path from untrusted text to runnable sandboxed wasm… where every executing stage is itself a wasm guest, running under wasmtime, never a native process. Lanes live one per language, and they share one framework instead of six bespoke integrations. Each lane is just a directory with a manifest, written in the grammar. Picture that manifest for Rust — six lines. Compiler, rust. The binary name, mrustc. Kind… compile to C, then wasm. The build script… build dot s-h. Target… wasm thirty-two wasi p-one. And the source… mrustc at a pinned commit. The load-bearing line is kind, and there are exactly four shapes a lane can be. First… compile and run — the tool both compiles and executes, like the tiny C-in-four-functions VM. Second… compile to C — emit C, then hand off, like Zig's C backend. Third… compile to wasm — produce a real wasm object, like clang and the mrustc chain. And fourth… interpret in sandbox — don't compile at all, just run an interpreter on the source, like yaegi for Go. Every one of those, a wasm guest at runtime.

tracks.title: Six lanes, three tricks
tracks.text: [excited] Now the whole layer on one picture. Six lanes, three tricks. Picture six source languages entering from the left. Two of them never reach a compiler at all — the c4 VM and yaegi short circuit straight to run. The rest each take a different dodge. Zig goes through zig1, which emits C. Rust goes through mrustc, which emits C. JavaScript becomes a C byte array. TypeScript runs through tsc inside QuickJS to become JavaScript… then becomes that same byte array. And here is the thing to watch. Almost everything funnels into the same two calls. Clang dash c, to make an object. Then wasm dash l d, to link it. And both of those… are one seventy-five megabyte LLVM multitool. So read it as three tricks. Interpret it — c4, yaegi, QuickJS. Transpile it to C — mrustc, zig1. Or run a real LLVM somebody already built for wasi — the keystone clang lane. Whatever the front half does, the back half is C. And C means clang… plus wasm-ld. C is the bottleneck language of the sandbox… by design.

tracks.title: The keystone — a linker that can't be spawned
tracks.text: The keystone — a linker that can't be spawned. Start here, because everything converges here. The production C lane is YoWASP clang and l l d, version twenty-two point one — LLVM built for the wasm target, so it runs on wasmtime. It's prebuilt and sha-pinned from an npm package. And it's one file, a seventy-five megabyte multitool, that dispatches on its first argument to act as either clang… or wasm-ld. Why clang and not something smaller? Because of one hard finding — no compiler without LLVM emits wasm. tcc and chibicc emit native code. c4 interprets. A real C-to-wasm compiler running inside wasm is, necessarily, LLVM. And then a wall shapes the whole lane — WASI has no fork. The clang driver cannot spawn a subprocess, so it cannot internally invoke the linker the way it normally would. So compile and link become two separate runs the host orchestrates by hand. Picture the sequence. First, the host runs the multitool as clang dash c, on hello dot c — out comes hello dot o, an object. The mounts are fixed every time — sysroot at slash usr, the job dir at slash work, slash tmp writable. Second, the host runs the same multitool as wasm-ld, linking that object with the C library, and an eight megabyte stack — because wasm-ld's default sixty-four kilobytes overflows on modest buffers. Out comes hello dot wasm. Third, wasmtime runs it… and prints ten… not equal… three million six hundred twenty-eight thousand eight hundred. A compiler also gets a raised budget — eight hundred billion fuel and a hundred eighty seconds, where an ordinary command gets five billion and thirty. Generous… but still a hard trap, not infinity. And multi-file builds compile their objects in parallel — worth about one point seven times on a real workload — a thirty-three file Lua build dropped from two hundred eighty seconds… to one sixty-six.

tracks.title: Rust without rustc
tracks.text: Rust without rustc — the crown jewel. The obvious move would be a rustc dot wasm. It doesn't exist, and it can't easily — for reasons that are a tour of the WASI walls. rustc embeds LLVM as a library. It shells out to a proc-macro server and a linker, as subprocesses — impossible without fork. It wants threads… and realpath… neither available under WASI. So the lane uses mrustc — a C plus plus program that compiles Rust to C. Built to wasm, it runs in-sandbox, and its C output goes into the clang lane. And the proof is real. Picture an honest little Rust program — a fib function, and a no-mangle export that returns fib of ten. Now walk the chain — six stages, every one a wasm guest. First, mrustc compiles libcore to C. Second, mrustc compiles the program to C. Third, clang compiles core dot c to an object. Fourth, clang compiles the program to an object. Fifth, wasm-ld links them with the C runtime and the builtins. And sixth, wasmtime runs the result… and prints… RUST IN WASM SANDBOX… fifty-five. fib of ten is fifty-five. And here's the kicker — the build peaked around six hundred megabytes. The wasm thirty-two four gigabyte ceiling everyone worries about… never bit. Full standard library works too — a program that prints HELLO FROM RUST STD IN WASM… forty-two. And the non-obvious part — libstd is prebuilt by mrustc itself, not by a native rustc, because hash and A-B-I consistency demand the same compiler build both. And if std isn't prebuilt? The lane returns an error — libstd not prebuilt — rather than silently shelling out to a native rustc. That refusal… is the doctrine in one return value.

tracks.title: The dependency frontier
tracks.text: [curious] The dependency frontier. Source compiling is table stakes. Dependencies are where it gets real. The Rust lane fetches crates from the crates dot i-o sparse index, and compiles them transitively, in-sandbox, same chain as your code. Twenty-three crates are proven — fnv, byteorder, base64, memchr, bitflags, smallvec, anyhow, once cell, and more. Let me give you the capability map as a verdict, not a grid. Pure source crates… work — twenty-three proven. Declarative macros, the macro-rules kind… work — mrustc expands them in pass. build dot rs autocfg probes… work — they're skipped, and the conservative fallback is correct. Version-pinned crates like regex and serde… work, with floors — the lane pins them to versions it knows compile. But two classes are still frontier. Proc-macro derives — like derive Serialize — have a bridge built, but it's ceiling-gated. And codegen build scripts… aren't solved yet. So about that ceiling. mrustc understands roughly Rust one point seven four today. Newer releases — syn two, edition twenty twenty-four — don't compile. The version floors hold the lane on versions that do. And proc-macros are the big unlock, and the hardest. mrustc natively pipes and spawns a proc-macro executable — forbidden under WASI. So the bridge compiles each proc-macro crate to a wasm server, speaking mrustc's own token protocol, and patches the spawn into a host import, running mrustc under Wasmex. It even spoofs the target — reporting the O-S as linux while the arch stays wasm — so syn's config guard passes. The bridge is built. But the fight is that same language ceiling. proc-macro2 runs in-sandbox today. The heavier syn-driven derives push right up against the frontier. We'd rather say that plainly than imply derive Serialize is uniformly green end to end. The whole remaining frontier is a short named list — codegen build scripts, proc-macros, the language ceiling, and runtime capabilities like tokio's networking and threads, routed to BEAM-mediated host imports. And the repo's own note on all of them is the one to keep — none are JIT-class walls.

tracks.title: The bootstrap compiler that only speaks C
tracks.text: Next — the bootstrap compiler that only speaks C. The Zig lane runs zig one — Zig's bootstrap compiler, version zero point sixteen. It runs the full Zig frontend, and the semantic analysis, and the C-backend codegen… all inside wasm… and emits C. Which takes the clang lane. zig1 is bootstrap only on purpose — every backend except the C backend is disabled, and the archiver and linker are stubbed out. It can do exactly one thing — build an object, format C. Which is precisely what this lane needs. There's a constraint — Zig resolves every path against a single preopen. So the lane stages the job directory beside the library under one root, and preopens the whole thing. Two committed bridges close the run step. One shim forwards the bare WASI externs Zig declares — like fd write and proc exit — onto wasi-libc. And a prelude no-ops two builtins Zig expects. Then a debug-print program runs… and prints zig-e2e… forty-two. A hello compile emits about eight hundred kilobytes of genuine Zig C output. And one subtle fix — an empty out dot c is now treated as a failed compile, because zig1 can emit a zero-byte file on error, which used to slip through as success and surface later as a confusing undefined-start error. The honest wall — going straight from Zig to wasm in-sandbox is blocked upstream. realpath isn't available on WASI, and there are open codegen bugs. So the lane goes through C… and says so.

tracks.title: Don't compile it at all
tracks.text: [mischievously] The Go lane takes the fourth trick — don't compile it at all. It runs yaegi, a pure-Go interpreter, cross-compiled to wasi once, by the native Go toolchain. And that native toolchain only ever builds the trusted runner — it never touches your code. The elegant bit is how your source rides in. The package manager glues your Go source into the runner as a wasm custom section, named wbgosrc. Picture the bytes — the yaegi runner… then a custom-section marker… then your source… then a length trailer, and a magic string, WBGOSRC1. This buys two things at once. Custom sections are ignored at execution — so the file is still a perfectly valid, runnable yaegi module. Nothing about the embedding breaks it. And because your source is now part of the bytes, every program is a unique, content-addressable, self-contained wasm — the runner pulls the source back out with a single read of that sixteen-byte trailer. No side files. The limit, verbatim — standard library only, no external module deps, single main package. Multi-file packages get merged into the one source yaegi evaluates.

tracks.title: Embed the interpreter per program
tracks.text: The JavaScript lane — embed the interpreter per program. This is the lane that bootstraps itself. QuickJS, version zero point ten, is compiled to wasm objects… by the clang lane. The sandbox builds its own JavaScript interpreter. Then each program embeds it. Your JS bytes become a C byte array — a const char array, your source as numbers, ending in zero — and the whole thing compiles and links into a standalone wasm, one per program. The link line glues the runtime, the harness, your source object, and the five QuickJS objects together. The bridge is the harness, which provides the Javy contract — read sync and write sync, bound directly onto wasi-libc read and write — plus console log, and a hand-rolled text encoder and decoder, because QuickJS ships neither. It deliberately skips the QuickJS POSIX library, whose environ and signals and popen don't exist under WASI. TypeScript reuses the whole stack — the real t-s-c runs inside QuickJS, takes TypeScript in, strips the types, and hands JavaScript to this lane. And then the speed valve. QuickJS is an interpreter, so bundling many files through it is slow. So the bundler routes esbuild first — esbuild compiled to wasi runs under wasmtime, which JITs it to native. [excited] A multi-file bundle that takes about twenty-three minutes interpreted in QuickJS… runs in about a hundred sixty milliseconds this way. It only falls back to the slow bundler when a Node core module needs the Dock shims.

tracks.title: The honest ledger
tracks.text: [curious] The honest ledger. The doctrine, quoted from the repo — done equals an honest answer per language. Each lane ships either a working in-sandbox compiler… or a committed honest-blocker note. No stubs. So here's the verdict, lane by lane. C is in-sandbox — its hard limit is the compile-link split, because there's no fork. Zig is in-sandbox — C backend only, direct-to-wasm blocked upstream. Rust is in-sandbox — bounded by the one point seven four ceiling, proc-macros gated. JavaScript is in-sandbox — it's an interpreter, so esbuild is the speed path. Go is in-sandbox — standard library only, single main package. TypeScript is in-sandbox — type-strip only, riding the JS lane. And then one holdout. jco — for typed component output — stays native, by design. It runs JavaScript under Node and wizer at build time, so it can't be a wasm guest. And that's acceptable, because those typed components are optional — the core dataflow uses the six in-sandbox lanes. But the most important honesty isn't a footnote — it's a return value. The old native build isolator was deleted, because with every untrusted compile in wasm, there's no native compile left to isolate. The wasm sandbox is the boundary now. And the native fallbacks were ripped out, not hidden — ask for a native Rust crate build, and you get an error — lane unavailable. Same for native Go, same for native Zig. The lane fails loudly… rather than quietly shelling out. A refusal you can see… beats a fallback you can't.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Can I use serde and derive Serialize? Pure source crates, yes — twenty-three proven. serde with a version floor compiles. The derives are the frontier — the bridge that runs proc-macros in-sandbox is built, but gated on the same one point seven four ceiling. Lean on declarative macros, and treat derives as in-progress. Why is my JS bundle fast — or slow? Routing. Multi-file bundles go through esbuild, which wasmtime JITs to native — about a hundred sixty milliseconds, where QuickJS would take twenty-three minutes. Can a malicious source escape during the compile? The compiler is just another sandboxed program — fixed preopens, bounded by fuel and a wall clock, job dir deleted after. There's no native build to attack, because there is no native build. Why not just bwrap the real rustc? Because the design doc calls that insufficient — a native compile under bwrap isn't a sufficient boundary for adversarial source. OS sandboxes are defense in depth, not isolation. And where do the compiler wasms come from? Trusted provisioning, once — native toolchains build only the trusted tools, never your code. The artifacts are gitignored, and DeployKit regenerates them.

tracks.title: Back up to toolkit
tracks.text: So that's lanes. The trick, in one breath — you don't need a language's official toolchain. You need any correct path from source to wasm, where every executing step is itself a wasm guest. Interpret it. Transpile it to C. Or run an LLVM somebody already built for wasi. And watch nearly everything funnel into the same two calls — clang, then wasm-ld. [curious] This was a deep dive under the toolkit lesson — so the way back up is short. Go to toolkit, lesson three, for the bet in two sentences. And then follow audits — the funnel that decides whether a tool even reaches a lane. The compiler runs in the sandbox. That's the whole bet.
